cards.explanation: The answer is to find a wife for Isaac. Abraham tells his chief servant to swear that he will take a wife for his son Isaac. Isaac is Abraham's son, so this oath is about his future family. I think that servant showed up expecting a normal work order, friends, and walked out with a whole matchmaking mission.

The answer is False. Abraham has the servant swear “…that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I am dwelling…” (Genesis 24:3). Then he says where to go instead: his own country and his kindred. Read past the word "not" and you've got the whole plan backwards, friends.

The answer is relatives. Abraham says the servant will go to “…my country and my kindred…” and kindred means family. So Isaac's wife is to come from Abraham's own people. And the servant has to find her without any group chat, friends. I'd have wanted a map and a cookie.

The answer is the land he lives in now. Abraham reminds the servant that the LORD promised him on oath to give this land to his offspring. "This land" is the one Abraham is living in right now. The same LORD who brought him out of his father's house made that promise, and Abraham leans on it as the servant heads out.

The answer is His angel. Abraham says the LORD, the God of heaven, “…will send His angel before you…” So the servant isn't heading out alone with ten camels and a big job. Abraham says an angel goes ahead of him on this search for a wife for Isaac.

The answer is True. Abraham says, “And if the woman is unwilling to follow you, then you are released from this oath of mine.” So the servant isn't stuck if the woman says no. But one thing stays put: “Only do not take my son back there.” The oath has an exit, and Isaac still doesn't go back.

The answer is the well. As evening approaches, the servant makes the camels kneel near the well outside the town. It's the time when the women go out to draw water. I think he picked a spot where people were sure to show up, and that's smart planning.

The answer is that she offers to water his camels too. The servant asks the LORD that the girl who answers his request for a drink with, “Drink, and I will water your camels as well” be the one appointed for Isaac. He's asking for more than a quick sip. That sign takes real kindness and real work, friends.

The answer is False. After Rebekah goes down to the spring, fills her jar and comes up again, the servant runs to meet her. Then he asks for a little water from her jar. He doesn't stand there waiting, friends, he RUNS.

The answer is True. Rebekah quickly empties her jar into the trough and runs back to the well to draw water. She keeps going until she has drawn water for all his camels. Ten camels and one jar, friends. I'd need a nap and a cookie just thinking about it.

The answer is that he's waiting to see if the LORD made his trip a success. The man watches her silently “to see whether or not the LORD had made his journey a success.” He prayed for success at the start, so he's watching to see how the LORD answers. I think that's a quiet kind of waiting, the kind where you don't want to say a word.

The answer is False. Genesis says, “And after the camels had finished drinking, he took out a gold ring weighing a beka, and two gold bracelets for her wrists weighing ten shekels.” The gifts come out after the last camel is done. He watched the whole job first, and only then did the gold come out.

The answer is that there's a place and plenty of feed. Rebekah says, “We have plenty of straw and feed, as well as a place for you to spend the night.” She says yes to the room, and she's thinking about the camels too. That's a generous answer, friends, and I'd say the camels were pleased.

The answer is His kindness and faithfulness to Abraham. The servant says, “…who has not withheld His kindness and faithfulness from my master.” He's thanking the LORD for how He has treated Abraham, the servant's master. Notice he puts the praise first, friends, before he says a word about himself.
